title: The Youngest Man in the Assembly
subtitle: New York, 1878–1886
intro: He walked into Albany at twenty-three in a tailored coat and got laughed at. Within a year he was calling for a judge's impeachment. Fifteen questions on Roosevelt's first taste of power — and the loss that ended it.

questions.prompt: How old was Roosevelt when he took his seat in the New York State Assembly?
questions.explanation: Twenty-three, and unmistakably the youngest member of the house. He deferred to nobody, which is not usually how a first term goes. Within weeks the older members had noticed him, mostly with irritation.

questions.prompt: Which Manhattan district sent him to Albany?
options: The Bowery and the Lower East Side tenement wards
Hell's Kitchen and the West Side rail yards
Harlem and the wards above Central Park
The Twenty-first, the silk stocking district
questions.explanation: The Twenty-first, a wealthy Republican district on the East Side that the press called the silk stocking district — the phrase was a jab at the money in it, and it stuck. Roosevelt won control of its Republican association by turning up to meetings that men of his class did not usually attend, in a room over a store, week after week, until the regulars stopped treating him as a visitor.
questions.imageAlt: Composite photograph of the New York State Assembly by the Notman Photo Company
questions.credit: New York State Assembly, composite photograph by the Notman Photo Company. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Where did Roosevelt begin his political career, learning the trade from the ground up?
questions.explanation: Morton Hall was the grandly named headquarters of the Twenty-first District Republican Association — a barn-sized room over a store, full of men his family would not have invited to dinner. He went anyway, and kept going until they took him seriously.
questions.imageAlt: The New York State Assembly, composite photograph
questions.credit: New York State Assembly, composite photograph by the Notman Photo Company. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: What made Roosevelt's name in his first term?
options: Demanding an investigation of a state judge
A bill to widen and fund the Erie Canal
Blocking the governor's budget in committee
A long speech attacking the protective tariff
questions.explanation: He went after Judge Theodore Westbrook over his handling of a case involving Jay Gould's elevated railway, calling for an investigation with a view to impeachment. It emerged that Westbrook's own son and cousin were employed by one of the receivers, and that Westbrook had written to Gould in terms no judge should have used about a litigant before him. The resolution failed, and the older members made sure the freshman knew it had failed. But the young assemblyman had made himself impossible to ignore, and the New York papers had a reformer to write about.

questions.prompt: What did Roosevelt's fellow legislators and the press call him early on?
questions.explanation: "Dude" — a dandy, an Easterner playing at something. It was aimed at his clothes, his voice, and his side-whiskers, and it was not affectionate. He got the same word thrown at him in Dakota a year later.

questions.prompt: How many one-year terms did Roosevelt serve in the Assembly?
questions.explanation: Three, from 1882 through 1884. Assembly terms in New York ran a single year, so he faced the voters each autumn. He chose not to seek a fourth.

questions.prompt: On February 14, 1884, while Roosevelt was in Albany, what happened?
options: His wife and his mother died on the same day
His own party stripped him of a committee chair
The Assembly chamber was gutted by fire
He resigned his seat without explanation
questions.explanation: Both women died in the same house, hours apart. His mother died of typhoid at three in the morning; his wife Alice died that afternoon of Bright's disease, two days after their daughter was born. In his diary he drew a heavy cross and wrote: "The light has gone out of my life." He went back to Albany within days and finished the session — chairing his committee, reporting his bills, saying nothing about any of it.

questions.prompt: At the 1884 Republican National Convention, Roosevelt backed a reform candidate against the front-runner. Who was his man?
questions.explanation: Roosevelt worked for Senator George Edmunds against James G. Blaine, who represented everything the reformers despised. Blaine won the nomination anyway.

questions.prompt: At that same 1884 convention, Roosevelt supported an African American delegate for temporary chairman. Who was he?
questions.explanation: John Roy Lynch of Mississippi, a former congressman born into slavery. Roosevelt spoke for him on the convention floor and Lynch was elected temporary chairman — a deliberate statement that the party of Lincoln still meant something, made by a man who was, at that moment, privately shattered.
questions.imageAlt: The New York State Assembly, composite photograph
questions.credit: New York State Assembly, composite photograph by the Notman Photo Company. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Many reform Republicans bolted the party rather than support Blaine. What did Roosevelt do?
options: Bolted with them and backed Cleveland
questions.explanation: The bolters became known as Mugwumps. Roosevelt, who privately loathed Blaine, stayed loyal to the ticket and campaigned for him. He calculated that a man who walks out has no party left to reform. It cost him friends, and he had doubts about it for years.

questions.prompt: In 1886 Roosevelt ran for mayor of New York City. How did he finish?
questions.explanation: Third, in a famous three-way race. Abram Hewitt won for the Democrats; the labour reformer Henry George came second; Roosevelt, the Republican, trailed. It was his most public failure to date — and it clarified for him that his future lay in national politics.
questions.imageAlt: The New York State Assembly, composite photograph
questions.credit: New York State Assembly, composite photograph by the Notman Photo Company. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Who was the third-party candidate who beat Roosevelt into second place in that mayoral race?
questions.explanation: Henry George, author of Progress and Poverty and the most influential economic radical in America, running as the United Labor candidate on a single tax on the value of land. His book had sold in the hundreds of thousands and his campaign pulled together trade unionists, Irish nationalists and socialists into something New York had not seen before. That a sitting Republican finished behind him tells you how volatile the city's politics were in 1886.

questions.prompt: What did Roosevelt do immediately after losing the 1886 mayoral election?
options: Sailed for London and married Edith Kermit Carow
Returned to the Badlands for good
Retired from public life for a decade
questions.explanation: He sailed on the Etruria with his sister Bamie — travelling as "Mr. and Miss Merrifield" to dodge reporters — and married Edith Kermit Carow at St George's, Hanover Square, on December 2, 1886. One account called it a wedding befitting a defeated mayoral candidate.

questions.credit: New York State Assembly, composite photograph by the Notman Photo Company. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: What did Roosevelt do with his infant daughter Alice after her mother's death?
options: Sent her to her Lee grandparents permanently
Placed her in the care of his sister Bamie
questions.explanation: His sister Anna — "Bamie" — took the baby and raised her for the first three years. Roosevelt could barely speak of Alice's mother afterwards, and almost never did. Bamie was unmarried and childless, and became the steadiest figure in the family.

questions.prompt: Between leaving the Assembly and returning to public office, what did Roosevelt do?
options: Took a diplomatic post at the Berlin legation
Practised law in a Wall Street firm
questions.explanation: He went west. Between 1884 and 1886 he ran cattle on the Little Missouri, served as a deputy sheriff, chaired a stockmen's association, and wrote a full-length biography of Thomas Hart Benton in a room above a store in Medora.
